upstream.sha_note: commit target of tag v0.2.2, which is also the default branch head at pin time.
upstream.provenance_note: The first grammar here that is not from tree-sitter/ or tree-sitter-grammars/: joker1007/tree-sitter-rbs is a single-maintainer repository, 15 stars, last pushed 2025-11-13. That was weighed rather than waved through — see grammar_assessment below for what was measured before vendoring it, and why writing our own was rejected.

generate_cli_note: same pin as the other grammars: tree-sitter-cli 0.26.x ships broken Unicode identifier tables (see treebank-rust ledger). Upstream generates cleanly under it, unlike php's master.

oracle.tool: tools/rbs-oracle/check.rb — RBS's own parser via RBS::Parser.parse_signature
oracle.note:
TWO-VALUED: valid / invalid. Parses and stops — no type checking, no constant resolution, and it never loads the signatures a file references, so a signature naming a class it cannot see is not an error and each file is judged on its own text.

THE VERSION IS LOAD-BEARING, more than for any other oracle here. Measured on this corpus of 2,216 files: rbs 2.8.2, the version bundled with CRuby 3.2, calls 48 of them invalid; rbs 4.1.3 calls 1. Forty-seven of the forty-eight were the toolchain rather than the files, and forty-six of those were the `rbs` gem's OWN core signatures, written in a syntax its own older parser predates. An oracle pinned to whatever ships with the interpreter would report this corpus 2% broken and file all of it as noise. check.rb therefore activates `gem "rbs", ">= 4.0"` and fails at startup rather than quietly judging RBS 4 by RBS 2's rules.
oracle.unreadable_note: An unreadable file is NOT an invalid file: check.rb writes the path and reason to stderr and exits 1 rather than emitting a verdict, so a mistyped corpus root fails the sweep instead of turning every grammar failure into noise.
oracle.not_ruby_note: RBS is not Ruby and the two oracles must never be crossed. `def foo(a) = a + 1` is Ruby and this parser rejects it; `def foo: (Integer) -> String` is RBS and CRuby rejects it. Both corpora come out of the same gems, which is exactly what makes the mistake easy.

smoke.build_note: --user-install because a CI runner and this VM both lack write access to the system gem directory, and rbs ships a native extension so it cannot be vendored as plain Ruby. The oracle activates  itself, so if this install is skipped or produces something older the oracle fails at startup rather than judging RBS 4 by RBS 2 rules.

patches.title: treebank crate identity
patches.origin: treebank; upstream owns the tree-sitter-rbs name on crates.io, so the redistribution publishes under its own: package name, repository, homepage and description. [lib] name stays tree_sitter_rbs so the crate is a drop-in replacement. include gains LOCAL-PATCHES.md, ledger.json and patches/* so provenance travels inside the published tarball. Upstream ships no Cargo.lock, so unlike the other grammars there is none to rename.

evidence.repro: def save!: () -> void  /  alias filter! select!
evidence.note: The single largest gap at 62 files. RBS's syntax doc gives both `?` and `!` as method-name suffixes and CRuby's rules are the same; only `?` was implemented. The precedence added with it is token-level rather than rule-level, and that distinction is the whole fix for `alias`: `filter!` is a LEXER choice between the immediate suffix and the `!` operator, which is itself a legal method name. `?` never had the ambiguity because there is no `?` operator. Rule-level prec was tried first and does not reach the decision. `alias ! not_op`, aliasing the operator itself, still parses.

Annotations were accepted on a top-level declaration (through `decl`) and on a member (through `member`), but a module or class body is `repeat(choice(member, _nestable_decls))` and the nested-declaration branch had none. So `%a{private}` before a nested interface — how rbs's own core signatures mark an internal interface — had nowhere to attach and failed the whole enclosing module.
Record and tuple types already allowed a trailing comma; type arguments did not. aws-sdk's generated signatures wrap long argument lists and leave one behind.

An integer literal type may carry a sign. A type position has no unary minus to fall back on, so the sign has to be part of the literal. rbs's core signatures use it for comparison results and language_server-protocol declares its LSP error codes as negative constants.

patches.title: bounded type parameters on a method type

evidence.note: A module's type parameters could carry an upper bound; a method's could not, so every bounded generic method failed. Variance and `unchecked` are deliberately NOT accepted here — RBS allows them only on a module's parameters, and RBS::Parser rejects `def f: [out T] () -> T`; test/negative/method-type-parameter-variance.rbs holds that. Inlined rather than given its own node so an unbounded parameter still parses to a bare type_variable and upstream's corpus tests keep passing unchanged.

patches.title: default for a module type parameter

evidence.repro: interface _Each[out T, out R = void]  /  class Thread::Queue[E = untyped]
evidence.note: Type parameter defaults were added in RBS 3.7 and are used throughout rbs's own core signatures. The grammar predates them.

`...` was accepted as a whole method type — 'this method's overloads are elsewhere' — but not as the TERMINATOR of a list. RBS allows both, and the terminating form is how aws-sdk's hand-written customizations extend generated signatures and how bigdecimal documents its numeric coercions.
An instance or class variable name may begin with an underscore, as it may in Ruby. Only a letter was accepted, so a module declaring one failed entirely.

A parameter name may be backtick-quoted, which is how RBS writes one that collides with a keyword. `method_name` already accepted the same quoting for a method called `class` or `include`; `var_name` did not.

corpus.source: RubyGems `.gem` files for the top gems by download count; `.rbs` files from the inner data.tar.gz. Identical acquisition to treebank-ruby, and `Lang::Rbs` delegates rank/resolve/archive handling to it rather than copying — RBS signatures ship inside gems, so the registry, the ranking and the nested-archive handling are the same problem with the same answer. Only classify() and validate() differ, which is the whole of what makes this a different language.
corpus.ranking: ecosyste.ms index of rubygems.org, sorted by downloads — the same list treebank-ruby uses.
corpus.files_note: .rbs only, the single extension tree-sitter-rbs's tree-sitter.json claims, and unambiguous: nothing else uses it. Paths containing a `vendor` component are excluded, as in ruby.
corpus.packages_note: 1000 gems fetched; 240 of them ship .rbs signatures at all. 2,214 files. The corpus is narrower than the file count suggests — rbs itself and language_server-protocol are ~32% of it — which is worth knowing when reading a gap count.
corpus.sweep_note: 93.1% -> 98.9%. noise_files is 0 at every patch level, which for this language means something stronger than usual: only ONE file in the whole corpus is oracle-invalid (http-form_data's `(Integer | void)`, a union RBS forbids), and the grammar accepts it — see grammar_looseness. So every failing file here is a genuine gap and gap_files is exact rather than a floor.
corpus.remaining_gaps_note: 24 files in 20 clusters remain, a long tail of 2s and 1s rather than anything systematic: inline type annotations in comments, a few keyword-quoted names in positions other than parameters, and assorted RBS 4.x syntax. 15 of the 24 are rbs's own core signatures, which is the same signal the assessment below records — this grammar trails RBS releases, and closing the tail is a subscription rather than a one-off.

grammar_looseness.summary: One construct RBS rejects that this grammar accepts: `void` inside a union type, e.g. `def rewind: () -> (Integer | void)`. It predates the treebank patches — verified against the pin with only the packaging patches applied.
grammar_looseness.why_this_is_safe: A sweep gap is 'grammar rejected it AND the oracle accepted it'. This runs the other way, so it cannot manufacture a gap. It is also the reason test/negative holds 19 files rather than 20: a negative-corpus file must be one the grammar actually rejects.
grammar_looseness.corpus_incidence: Exactly one file in the top-1000 gem corpus, http-form_data-3.0.1/sig/http/form_data/readable.rbs, which is also the only oracle-invalid file in the entire corpus.

grammar_assessment.summary: joker1007/tree-sitter-rbs is the first grammar vendored here that is not from tree-sitter/ or tree-sitter-grammars/: 15 stars, one maintainer, v0.2.2, last pushed 2025-11-13. ROADMAP.md treats that profile as a blocker rather than a footnote, so it was measured before being adopted rather than after.
grammar_assessment.what_was_measured: Out of the box it parsed 93.14% of the corpus. Against 22 structurally-plausible but invalid signatures — a lowercase class name, `interface Foo` without the underscore, `type Foo = Integer`, `class C < 3`, `def f:: () -> void` — it wrongly accepted ZERO. Its trees carry named fields (name, body, superclass, type_parameters) and node names lifted from RBS's own vocabulary (generics_bound, bound_type, ivar_member), which is someone working from the spec rather than pattern-matching until tests pass. It ships 133 corpus tests of its own and generates cleanly under our pinned CLI 0.25.10.
grammar_assessment.why_not_write_our_own: Considered and rejected. RBS's reference parser is 4,258 lines of C against a 940-line syntax spec; upstream covers that in 489 lines of grammar.js at 93% before any patch, so it is near-complete rather than a stub. Writing our own would re-derive all of it plus the 133 tests to land near where a submodule pin already puts us, and it would break the model DESIGN.md states — the patches are the offer. Eleven patches against joker1007's grammar are a contribution he can take; a treebank-authored grammar is a fork nobody upstreams.
grammar_assessment.the_standing_risk: Not fixable by patching: 15 of the 24 remaining gaps are rbs's own core signatures, so the grammar trails RBS releases and will keep drifting as Ruby core evolves the language. If that drift outpaces the patch series, forking is the fallback — but it should be a decision taken on evidence, not the opening move.
